notes: De Jong cabinet = KVP (ruling slot 1) + VVD (slot 2) + ARP + CHU. ARP takes slot 14 (popularity 0.10, close to its 9.9 percent); CHU takes slot 13 as the regents' party of Crown-appointed mayors and administrators (popularity 0.08, close to its 8.1 percent). SGP therefore moves from MD slot 14 to slot 6 as the Calvinist reactionaries (keeps its MD sprite). D'66 stays in MD slot 18. Date switches: small-business milieu -> NMP (Sept 1970, day approximate), MLCN -> SP (1972.10.22), Sint Martinusfonds -> NVU (1971.3.27). Not placed: GPV, PPR, DS'70 (founded April 1970), Kabouters (Feb 1970).

0.name: Binnenlandse Veiligheidsdienst
0.text:
The National Security Service was created in 1949 under the Ministry of the Interior, growing out of the security bureaus that hunted collaborators after the liberation. Its first chief, the former police officer Louis Einthoven, built it into a discreet anti-communist apparatus with informers deep inside the CPN, and it now also watches Provo veterans, Maoist splinters, radical students and Moluccan exiles.

The service sees the Netherlands as a NATO frontline state threatened by subversion from within. It shares intelligence with the CIA and allied services, vets civil servants and keeps files on thousands of citizens. Answerable only to the Interior minister, it would be the natural backbone of a firm Atlanticist government ready to put order before liberty.

1.name: Katholieke Volkspartij
1.text:
The Catholic People's Party is the political arm of Catholic Netherlands, heir to the pre-war Roman Catholic State Party. It leads the cabinet of Prime Minister Piet de Jong in coalition with the VVD, ARP and CHU, while Norbert Schmelzer leads its deputies. Yet the party is shaken: the 1967 election cost it eight seats, and in 1968 left-wing dissidents broke away to found the PPR.

The KVP stands for Catholic social teaching, the welfare state built under ministers such as Marga Klompé, European integration and firm loyalty to NATO, embodied by Foreign Minister Joseph Luns. Its base is the Catholic south, the Catholic unions and farmers' leagues. Talks with the ARP and CHU on a joint Christian democratic front are its answer to secularisation.

2.name: Volkspartij voor Vrijheid en Democratie
2.english: People's Party for Freedom and Democracy
2.text:
The People's Party for Freedom and Democracy was founded in 1948 as the party of secular liberalism. Since 1967 it has served as junior partner in the De Jong cabinet, providing Finance Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Johan Witteveen and Justice Minister Carel Polak. Its parliamentary group is led by Molly Geertsema, Haya van Someren chairs the party, and the combative young deputy Hans Wiegel is a rising star.

The VVD champions private enterprise, sound public finances, lower taxes and individual responsibility, and it is unwaveringly Atlanticist and pro-European. It draws on business, the professions and the secular middle classes of the Randstad. Small in numbers but indispensable to any centre-right majority, it hopes to profit as the old religious pillars crumble.
2.wiki: People's Party for Freedom and Democracy

3.name: Partij van de Arbeid
3.text:
The Labour Party was founded in 1946 to break through the old religious pillars and has been in opposition since the Night of Schmelzer brought down the Cals cabinet in 1966. Joop den Uyl, economics minister in that cabinet, leads it in parliament. Since 1966 the Nieuw Links (New Left) movement has captured much of the apparatus, and in 1969 the party chose Anne Vondeling as its chairman.

Labour stands for a fairer distribution of income, knowledge and power, a strong welfare state and democratisation of workplaces. Under New Left pressure it has vowed not to govern with the KVP and seeks a progressive bloc with D'66 and the PPR, while questioning the Vietnam War and NATO's nuclear strategy. Its base is the NVV unions and the secular working class.

4.name: Communistische Partij van Nederland
4.text:
The Communist Party of the Netherlands, founded in 1909 as a left split from social democracy, holds five seats and is strongest in Amsterdam, the Zaan district and the peat colonies of East Groningen. Its long-time strongman Paul de Groot, now honorary chairman, steered it onto an 'autonomous' course after 1963, distancing it from both Moscow and Beijing; Henk Hoekstra chairs the party and Marcus Bakker leads its deputies.

The CPN is orthodox Marxist-Leninist in organisation but fiercely independent: it condemned the 1968 invasion of Czechoslovakia and accepts no foreign tutelage. It campaigns for higher wages and rent control, for withdrawal from NATO and against the American war in Vietnam. Its daily De Waarheid, its youth league and a loyal core of industrial workers form its base.

5.name: Pacifistisch Socialistische Partij
5.text:
The Pacifist Socialist Party was founded in 1957 by Christian pacifists, left-wing socialists and former communists who rejected both NATO and the Soviet bloc. Henk Lankhorst long led its group in parliament; it now holds four seats, with younger deputies such as Bram van der Lek reflecting a generation radicalised by the Vietnam War, Provo and the 1969 student occupations.

The PSP demands unilateral nuclear disarmament, withdrawal from NATO, support for liberation movements in the Third World and a socialism built on workers' self-management rather than state bureaucracy. Its youth and student branches overlap with anarchists, Trotskyist entrists and anti-colonial activists. Weak in parliament, it is strong on the streets, in the universities and in the protest press, and sets the tone for the radical left.

6.name: Staatkundig Gereformeerde Partij
6.text:
The Reformed Political Party was founded in 1918 by the Reverend Gerrit Hendrik Kersten to bring the strictest Calvinism into politics. It holds three seats, led in the Tweede Kamer by the veteran Cornelis van Dis, and draws unshakeable votes from the 'Bible Belt' of orthodox Reformed villages running from Zeeland through the Betuwe to Staphorst.

The SGP wants a state governed by God's commandments as laid down in the original Belgic Confession and rejects popular sovereignty. It opposes women in political office, Sunday work, compulsory vaccination and the permissive society, and distrusts European integration as a Catholic project. Fiercely anti-communist and devoted to the House of Orange, it never joins governments but remains the unbending voice of Protestant reaction against the secular age.

7.name: De Moskougetrouwen
7.text:
The Moscow Loyalists are the orthodox communists who never accepted Paul de Groot's break with the Soviet party in the 1960s. They survive as a quiet minority in CPN branches, among veteran trade unionists of the dissolved Unity Trade Union Centre and in friendship and peace committees that keep up contacts with the Soviet embassy and East German trade offices.

For them De Groot's 'autonomy' and the CPN's condemnation of the 1968 intervention in Czechoslovakia are a betrayal of proletarian internationalism. They look to the Soviet Union as the guarantor of socialism, want the Netherlands out of NATO and admire the disciplined vanguard states of Eastern Europe. Their leverage lies in Soviet goodwill, trade contacts and the hope that De Groot's succession will reopen the door to Moscow.

8.name: Anjoman-e Eslami-ye Delft
8.text:
The Islamic Society of Delft is a small circle of Iranian engineering students at the Delft Institute of Technology and the agricultural college at Wageningen, joined by a few Iranian doctors working in Dutch hospitals. Apart from the secular and Maoist Iranian student confederation, they meet for Friday prayers and Muharram gatherings in rented rooms and pass around the writings of Mehdi Bazargan, the engineer who founded the Freedom Movement of Iran.

Their ideal is a modern, rational Shia Islam compatible with science, constitutional government and social justice. They oppose the Shah's autocracy and his dependence on the United States, but also distrust communism and clerical obscurantism. Their influence lies in their education: they expect to return home as engineers and teachers of a reformed faith.

9.name: Hey'at-e Hosseini
9.text:
The Husayni Circle is a mourning association of a few dozen Iranian and Iraqi Shia in Rotterdam and The Hague: merchants in the oil and carpet trade, seamen from tankers calling at Europoort and a handful of students. Each Muharram they gather to lament the martyrdom of Imam Husayn, and their preachers read out the sermons and letters of Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, exiled to Najaf since 1965.

The circle holds that the Shah is a tyrant serving America and Israel and that the learned clergy, not kings or parliaments, must guide Muslim society. It shuns the secular Iranian opposition abroad and sends religious dues to Khomeini's representatives. Its weight in Dutch politics is nil, but it is a link in the chain that binds exiled clerics to believers across Europe.

10.name: Ahl al-Bay'a
10.text:
The People of the Allegiance are the Moroccan workers who keep faith with King Hassan II as Commander of the Faithful. Recruited under the labour agreement signed with Morocco in 1969, they live in boarding houses in Amsterdam, Rotterdam and Utrecht, pray in rooms lent by employers, and are watched over by the Moroccan embassy and consulates, which supply imams and Korans.

Their Islam is that of the Moroccan state: Maliki, Sufi-tinged, obedient to the throne and hostile to both leftist agitation and revolutionary Islamism. They want prayer rooms, halal meat, Arabic lessons for their children and the right to return home with their savings. Their leverage lies in the Moroccan state, which needs their remittances and will not let them drift into the orbit of the exiled left-wing opposition.

11.name: Shabab al-Khilafa
11.text:
The Youth of the Caliphate is a cell of half a dozen Jordanian and Palestinian students at Delft and Wageningen who spread the ideas of Hizb ut-Tahrir, the Liberation Party founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by Taqi al-Din al-Nabhani. Banned in Jordan and most of the Arab world, the party survives through such student cells abroad; they meet in dormitories and hand out duplicated pamphlets after Friday prayers.

They teach that the defeat of 1967 proves the bankruptcy of Arab nationalism and that only a restored caliphate ruling by the sharia can unite the Muslims and liberate Palestine. Democracy, socialism and Western capitalism are all rejected as man-made systems. Their influence among Dutch Muslims is minimal, but their discipline and secrecy make them the seed of future networks.

12.name: Keluarga Bulan Bintang
12.text:
The Crescent and Star Family takes its name from the emblem of Masyumi, the great Indonesian modernist Muslim party that Sukarno banned in 1960. In The Hague, Leiden and Amsterdam its Dutch circle unites Indonesian students, former colonial civil servants and Dutch-Indonesian Muslims who revere Masyumi's leader Mohammad Natsir, released from prison in 1966 and now head of the Indonesian Islamic Propagation Council.

Like the Muslim Brotherhood, with which Natsir has close ties through the Muslim World League, the circle preaches an Islam that is modern, educated and politically engaged, compatible with parliamentary democracy and fiercely anti-communist. It resents Suharto's refusal to let Masyumi return, organises study evenings and charity, and dreams of a Muslim youth union spanning all of Europe.

13.name: Christelijk-Historische Unie
13.text:
The Christian Historical Union, founded in 1908, is the party of moderate Protestants in the Netherlands Reformed Church and the most establishment-minded of the three religious parties. It holds twelve seats and two cabinet posts: Interior Minister Henk Beernink and Berend Udink, minister for development aid. Out of all proportion to its vote, CHU men sit in town halls as Crown-appointed mayors and in the high councils of state, among them Jan de Pous, chairman of the Social and Economic Council.

The CHU distrusts ideology, preferring authority, sound administration, the monarchy and the Protestant character of the nation. It is loyal to NATO but wary of merging with the Catholics. Its strength is that of a governing class: notables who run the provinces whoever wins elections.

14.name: Anti-Revolutionaire Partij
14.text:
The Anti-Revolutionary Party, founded in 1879 by Abraham Kuyper, is the oldest party in the Netherlands and the political home of the orthodox Reformed churches. With fifteen seats it is a pillar of the De Jong cabinet, supplying Deputy Prime Minister Joop Bakker and Social Affairs Minister Bauke Roolvink, while former agriculture minister Barend Biesheuvel leads its parliamentary group.

Its name recalls its founding rejection of the French Revolution's sovereignty of man, but the modern ARP is a socially engaged Christian democratic party: committed to the welfare state, development aid and NATO, and increasingly critical of apartheid and the Vietnam War. Rooted in the CNV unions, the Free University of Amsterdam and the daily Trouw, it is negotiating closer cooperation with the KVP and CHU.

15.name: Verbond van Nederlandse Ondernemingen
15.text:
The Federation of Netherlands Industry was formed in 1968 by merging the two secular employers' federations, the Federation of Dutch Employers and the Central Social Employers' Federation. It speaks for the great multinationals that dominate the Dutch economy, Royal Dutch Shell, Unilever, Philips, AKZO and the Hoogovens steelworks, together with the shipping, banking and port interests of Rotterdam and Amsterdam.

Within the consensus machinery of the Social and Economic Council it bargains with unions and government over wages, prices and social charges, pressing for wage restraint, free trade, a strong guilder and European integration. Atlanticist and anti-socialist, it fears the New Left and wildcat strikes. Its leverage is immense: jobs, investment and direct access to ministers through a dense web of board seats.

16.name: Het Middenstandsverzet
16.text:
The Shopkeepers' Revolt is the anger of the Dutch middenstand: grocers, bakers, garage owners, craftsmen and independent hauliers squeezed by rising social premiums, red tape and the value-added tax introduced on 1 January 1969, which brought price controls and mountains of paperwork. Entrepreneurs such as Martin Dessing and Ab te Pas give voice to the grievances of the self-employed.

They want a fairer distribution of burdens between entrepreneurs and employees, lower taxes, less bureaucracy and an end to state direction of the economy, and they decry inflation and street disorder alike. They feel abandoned by the VVD as a party of big business and by the corporatism of the religious parties. Their leverage lies in hundreds of thousands of small proprietors.

16.name: Nederlandse Middenstands Partij
16.text:
The Dutch Middle Class Party was founded in September 1970 by three entrepreneurs, Martin Dessing, Ab te Pas and H. Kamping, to turn the discontent of shopkeepers, craftsmen and the self-employed into votes. It is a pure interest party and aims to enter the Tweede Kamer at the next general election.

Its programme calls first for a better, fairer and more acceptable distribution of burdens for entrepreneurs, the self-employed and the middle classes, together with an end to state direction of the economy, bureaucracy and inflation, and firm action against 'anarchy' in the streets. It is Atlanticist by instinct but largely indifferent to foreign policy. Its leverage lies in a protest electorate that the VVD and the confessional parties take for granted.

17.name: Vereniging tot Behoud van Natuurmonumenten in Nederland
17.english: Society for the Preservation of Nature Monuments
17.native_full: Vereniging tot Behoud van Natuurmonumenten in Nederland
17.text:
The Society for the Preservation of Nature Monuments was founded in 1905 by the teachers and naturalists Jac. P. Thijsse and Eli Heimans, and won its first fight in 1906 by buying the Naardermeer lake to stop Amsterdam turning it into a rubbish dump. It now owns and manages dozens of reserves of heath, dune, fen and woodland and counts tens of thousands of members.

The society is politically neutral but increasingly drawn into battles over the price of growth: motorways, the planned Markerwaard polder, industrial pollution of the Rhine and schemes to dam estuaries and reclaim the Wadden Sea. Its weapons are land purchase, expert reports and a respectable middle-class membership that ministers cannot ignore, and it is the backbone of a fast-growing environmental awareness.

18.name: Democraten '66
18.text:
Democrats 66 was founded in October 1966 by the journalist Hans van Mierlo and a group of young professionals determined to 'explode' the old party system. In its first election in 1967 it won a sensational seven seats, and van Mierlo leads its parliamentary group with an informal, televisual style that appeals to young, educated and secular voters.

D'66 is pragmatic and anti-dogmatic rather than socialist or liberal in the classic sense. Its central demands are constitutional: a directly elected prime minister, a district electoral system and an end to pillarised power-sharing behind closed doors. It is pro-European and loyal to NATO while critical of the Vietnam War, and it is exploring a progressive alliance with Labour and the PPR.

19.name: Marxistisch-Leninistisch Centrum Nederland
19.text:
The Marxist-Leninist Centre of the Netherlands grew out of a pro-Chinese faction in the CPN whose leading figures, Nico Schrevel and Daan Monjé, were expelled at the end of 1964. It has a small but intense following of workers and students, and this month it reorganises itself as the Communist Unity Movement of the Netherlands (Marxist-Leninist).

It follows Mao Zedong Thought, denounces the Soviet Union as social-imperialist and the CPN as revisionist, and calls for a disciplined vanguard to prepare revolution against American imperialism and Dutch monopoly capital. Its activists sell Chinese literature at factory gates and court students radicalised in 1969. Tension is growing between its intellectuals and a proletarian wing that wants to work among ordinary people.
19.wiki: Communist Unity Movement of the Netherlands (Marxist–Leninist)

19.name: Socialistiese Partij
19.text:
The Socialist Party took its present name in October 1972, a year after Daan Monjé led the 'proletarian' majority out of the Communist Unity Movement to found the Communist Party of the Netherlands (Marxist-Leninist). Rejecting student intellectualism, its cadres moved into working-class districts, with early strongholds in Nijmegen and Oss.

The SP remains Maoist in doctrine, but its practice is local and practical: action committees on housing, rents, pollution and health care, and help for ordinary people with grievances against landlords and authorities. It denounces both superpowers, and NATO and the EEC as instruments of big capital. Its leverage lies in disciplined grassroots work that the older left parties have abandoned.

20.name: Boerenpartij
20.text:
The Farmers' Party was founded in 1958 by Hendrik Koekoek, a farmer who led the 'free farmers' in refusing compulsory levies to the corporatist Agricultural Board. 'Boer Koekoek' became a television sensation and in 1967 his party won seven seats, but the group has since been torn by quarrels and splits, while former members of the wartime NSB on its lists have caused repeated scandals.

The party is a Dutch variant of Poujadism: it attacks taxes, bureaucracy, the welfare state, the regulated agricultural economy and the 'regents' of all established parties. It is anti-communist, nationalist and suspicious of the EEC and of permissive youth culture. Its voters are farmers, shopkeepers and protest voters in the countryside and the new suburbs, and its weapon is anger at The Hague.

21.name: Stichting Sint Martinusfonds
21.text:
The Saint Martin's Fund was set up in 1953 as a mutual aid foundation for Dutch veterans of the Waffen-SS and their families: the men who volunteered for the Eastern Front and were imprisoned and stripped of their citizenship after the liberation. It publishes a members' bulletin, organises reunions and keeps up contacts with veterans' circles in West Germany and Flanders.

Officially charitable, the fund nurses a revisionist memory of the occupation, presenting its members as idealistic anti-communist crusaders betrayed by the postwar purge. It seeks pension rights, rehabilitation and an end to the stigma attached to 'wrong' families. It has no party of its own, but its networks link the old National Socialist milieu to young activists searching for a new far-right organisation.

21.name: Nederlandse Volks-Unie
21.text:
The Dutch People's Union was founded on 27 March 1971 by activists of the Aktiegroep Vlaanderen and the Nieuw Rechts Front, small radical nationalist groups seeking a political vehicle. It aims to give the Dutch far right a party of its own, drawing on old collaborators, Greater Netherlands nationalists and disaffected youths.

The NVU preaches 'people's nationalism': the unity of the Dutch and the Flemings in one Dietse nation, an authoritarian corporative state, and hostility to communism, parliamentary 'chaos' and guest-worker immigration. It flirts with the symbols of the wartime NSB and is shadowed by the security service and anti-fascist groups. Its leverage is minimal, but it gives the far right a public face and a list for elections.

22.name: Nederlandse krijgsmacht
22.text:
The Netherlands Armed Forces are a large conscript force fully integrated into NATO. The I Netherlands Army Corps is committed to the defence of the North German plain, the Royal Netherlands Navy patrols the eastern Atlantic and the Caribbean, and Prince Bernhard serves as Inspector-General of the armed forces. In May 1969 marines restored order in Willemstad after the Curaçao riots.

The officer corps is professional, Atlanticist and firmly subordinate to civilian rule, but uneasy: budgets are under pressure, the New Left mocks the military, and the conscripts' union VVDM, founded in 1966, campaigns for long hair, better pay and the abolition of saluting. Its leverage lies in its NATO ties, royal patronage and the respect it commands among older Dutch voters.

23.name: Huis Oranje-Nassau
23.text:
The House of Orange-Nassau has headed the Dutch state since 1813 and personifies national unity. Queen Juliana, on the throne since 1948, is a homely, socially concerned monarch; her husband Prince Bernhard is Inspector-General of the armed forces, founder of the Bilderberg meetings and a tireless promoter of Dutch business abroad. Crown Princess Beatrix's 1966 marriage to the German diplomat Claus von Amsberg drew Provo smoke bombs, but the birth of Willem-Alexander in 1967 secured the succession.

The monarchy reigns rather than rules, yet the Queen appoints the informateurs and formateurs who build every cabinet, and the royal family's Atlanticist and business connections are formidable. Republicanism is confined to the radical left, while Orange sentiment remains strong among Protestants and ordinary Dutch people.
